passages: CAMP HILL, Pa.--( BUSINESS WIRE )--Forma Medical Inc. announced today that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued U.S. Patent No. 12,751,749, titled “System for Joint Fixation of Extremity Bone and Related Methods.” The patent, which issued October 6, 2026, covers surgical methods for what Forma calls minimally invasive plate arthrodesis, or MIPA™, in which a plate is introduced and secured across a joint of the foot through small incisions rather than a traditional open exposure.

Fusion surgery, or arthrodesis, permanently joins two bones across a joint damaged by arthritis or deformity. It is a mainstay of foot and ankle reconstruction at the big toe, the midfoot, and the hindfoot. Surgeons have long faced a trade-off in how they perform it. Plates provide stable, well-established fixation but have traditionally required a longer incision to implant. Minimally invasive techniques shrink the incision but have typically relied on a screw-only construct. MIPA is designed to remove that trade-off.

The name echoes a shift in fracture care. Since the 1990s, orthopedic trauma surgeons have adopted minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis (MIPO), sliding fracture plates beneath the skin through small incisions to protect the surrounding soft tissue and blood supply. MIPA applies the same principles to joint fusion.

“The fixation surgeons trust, through the small incisions patients ask for. That is what surgeons told us they needed, and MIPA is designed to deliver both,” said Andrew C. Davison, CEO of Forma Medical. “This patent covers the method, not a single implant. The big toe was our starting point, with more than 1,000 procedures to date. The claims extend to other joints of the foot where surgeons already reach for a plate.”

“In urgent fracture care, we have evolved to less invasive surgical approaches for internal fixation, with less anatomic distortion and soft tissue dissection,” said Jesse F. Doty, MD, FAAOS, a fellowship-trained orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon at Integrity Orthopedics and Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery at the University of Tennessee and a co-inventor of the patented technology. “Elective fusion has been slower to progress to an established equivalent until now. MIPA offers a defined, repeatable way to deliver more robust plate fixation through smaller incisions, providing the same benefits we've seen from minimally invasive surgery in other anatomic areas, but without compromised stability. I’ve used MIPA for MTP joint fusions in my own practice for years now. My experience and patient feedback have been highly encouraging, and I plan to submit my clinical outcomes for publication later this year.”

About Forma Medical Forma Medical Inc. is a privately held orthopedic device company focused on developing differentiated solutions that combine strong biomechanical principles with minimally invasive surgical techniques. The company’s flagship OptimalMTP® system is designed to advance the standard of care in first MTP joint fusion by delivering stability, reproducibility, and efficiency through an MIS approach. OptimalMTP received FDA 510(k) clearance in 2024 and has been used in more than 1,000 procedures.
James A. Gault Forma Medical support@formamedical.com

passages: CAMP HILL, Pa.--( BUSINESS WIRE )--Forma Medical Inc. announced today that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued U.S. Patent No. 12,751,749, titled “System for Joint Fixation of Extremity Bone and Related Methods.” The patent, which issued October 6, 2026, covers surgical methods for what Forma calls minimally invasive plate arthrodesis, or MIPA™, in which a plate is introduced and secured across a joint of the foot through small incisions rather than a traditional open exposure.

Fusion surgery, or arthrodesis, permanently joins two bones across a joint damaged by arthritis or deformity. It is a mainstay of foot and ankle reconstruction at the big toe, the midfoot, and the hindfoot. Surgeons have long faced a trade-off in how they perform it. Plates provide stable, well-established fixation but have traditionally required a longer incision to implant. Minimally invasive techniques shrink the incision but have typically relied on a screw-only construct. MIPA is designed to remove that trade-off.

The name echoes a shift in fracture care. Since the 1990s, orthopedic trauma surgeons have adopted minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis (MIPO), sliding fracture plates beneath the skin through small incisions to protect the surrounding soft tissue and blood supply. MIPA applies the same principles to joint fusion.

“The fixation surgeons trust, through the small incisions patients ask for. That is what surgeons told us they needed, and MIPA is designed to deliver both,” said Andrew C. Davison, CEO of Forma Medical. “This patent covers the method, not a single implant. The big toe was our starting point, with more than 1,000 procedures to date. The claims extend to other joints of the foot where surgeons already reach for a plate.”

“In urgent fracture care, we have evolved to less invasive surgical approaches for internal fixation, with less anatomic distortion and soft tissue dissection,” said Jesse F. Doty, MD, FAAOS, a fellowship-trained orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon at Integrity Orthopedics and Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery at the University of Tennessee and a co-inventor of the patented technology. “Elective fusion has been slower to progress to an established equivalent until now. MIPA offers a defined, repeatable way to deliver more robust plate fixation through smaller incisions, providing the same benefits we've seen from minimally invasive surgery in other anatomic areas, but without compromised stability. I’ve used MIPA for MTP joint fusions in my own practice for years now. My experience and patient feedback have been highly encouraging, and I plan to submit my clinical outcomes for publication later this year.”

About Forma Medical Forma Medical Inc. is a privately held orthopedic device company focused on developing differentiated solutions that combine strong biomechanical principles with minimally invasive surgical techniques. The company’s flagship OptimalMTP® system is designed to advance the standard of care in first MTP joint fusion by delivering stability, reproducibility, and efficiency through an MIS approach. OptimalMTP received FDA 510(k) clearance in 2024 and has been used in more than 1,000 procedures.

extraction.body: SpaceX is planning to go public this summer, and the initial public offering (IPO) will almost certainly be the biggest of all time. The company is targeting a $1.75 trillion valuation and a listing size of $70 billion to $75 billion. Considering the immense hype and the high valuation baked into that market cap, SpaceX shares will be a risky investment -- even for those retail investors who are able to join the big players and get them at the IPO price. But there are two tech stocks trading at more reasonable prices that also stand to benefit from the IPO. Alphabet ( GOOG -1.08% ) ( GOOGL -1.24% ) , the company that owns Google, invested in SpaceX during its Series F funding round in 2015. It paid $900 million at a $12 billion valuation, giving it about a 7.5% stake in the space company. SpaceX has held multiple funding rounds since then and issued additional shares, diluting Alphabet's position. However, it still had a 6.11% stake at the end of 2025, according to a regulatory filing. If that hasn't changed and SpaceX goes public at a $1.75 trillion valuation, Alphabet's position will be worth about $107 billion. Alphabet stock has been on a fantastic run lately, surging by 140% over the last 12 months (as of May 15) and adding trillions to its market cap. Its SpaceX position isn't exactly a game changer, but it does add extra upside to Alphabet's strong core businesses. And at 28 times forward earnings, Alphabet doesn't trade at an expensive valuation, particularly given it's one of the top tech stocks on the market. Nvidia ( NVDA -0.59% ) didn't have as much to gain from the SpaceX IPO until February, when the space company acquired xAI, which was also controlled by CEO Elon Musk. In the wake of that acquisition, SpaceX now owns xAI's Colossus data center, which houses over 220,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs). SpaceX rents out Colossus capacity to artificial intelligence (AI) companies , including Anthropic. That's not xAI's only connection to Nvidia. Last year, xAI became the first customer for a Saudi Arabian data center that features about 600,000 Nvidia GPUs. Because of xAI, SpaceX will need still more chips, and a $75 billion initial stock sale will provide it with cash to continue expanding its AI infrastructure. Nvidia is currently SpaceX's main chip supplier, and based on Musk's comments, that arrangement is staying in place. Musk has said that he's a "huge admirer" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and that SpaceX and Tesla will both continue to buy large quantities of Nvidia chips. Nvidia has also grown rapidly over the past year, up about 63% to a market cap of $5.4 trillion. But like Alphabet, its valuation is lower than you might think. It trades at 26 times forward earnings, so it's not too late to buy Nvidia stock, especially with the potential for even larger orders from SpaceX after it goes public. The company is targeting a $1.75 trillion valuation and a listing size of $70 billion to $75 billion. Considering the immense hype and the high valuation baked into that market cap, SpaceX shares will be a risky investment -- even for those retail investors who are able to join the big players and get them at the IPO price. But there are two tech stocks trading at more reasonable prices that also stand to benefit from the IPO. Alphabet ( GOOG -1.08% ) ( GOOGL -1.24% ) , the company that owns Google, invested in SpaceX during its Series F funding round in 2015. It paid $900 million at a $12 billion valuation, giving it about a 7.5% stake in the space company. SpaceX has held multiple funding rounds since then and issued additional shares, diluting Alphabet's position. However, it still had a 6.11% stake at the end of 2025, according to a regulatory filing. If that hasn't changed and SpaceX goes public at a $1.75 trillion valuation, Alphabet's position will be worth about $107 billion. Alphabet stock has been on a fantastic run lately, surging by 140% over the last 12 months (as of May 15) and adding trillions to its market cap. Its SpaceX position isn't exactly a game changer, but it does add extra upside to Alphabet's strong core businesses. And at 28 times forward earnings, Alphabet doesn't trade at an expensive valuation, particularly given it's one of the top tech stocks on the market. Nvidia ( NVDA -0.59% ) didn't have as much to gain from the SpaceX IPO until February, when the space company acquired xAI, which was also controlled by CEO Elon Musk. In the wake of that acquisition, SpaceX now owns xAI's Colossus data center, which houses over 220,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs). SpaceX rents out Colossus capacity to artificial intelligence (AI) companies , including Anthropic. That's not xAI's only connection to Nvidia. Last year, xAI became the first customer for a Saudi Arabian data center that features about 600,000 Nvidia GPUs. Because of xAI, SpaceX will need still more chips, and a $75 billion initial stock sale will provide it with cash to continue expanding its AI infrastructure. Nvidia is currently SpaceX's main chip supplier, and based on Musk's comments, that arrangement is staying in place. Musk has said that he's a "huge admirer" of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and that SpaceX and Tesla will both continue to buy large quantities of Nvidia chips. Nvidia has also grown rapidly over the past year, up about 63% to a market cap of $5.4 trillion. But like Alphabet, its valuation is lower than you might think. It trades at 26 times forward earnings, so it's not too late to buy Nvidia stock, especially with the potential for even larger orders from SpaceX after it goes public. The company's artificial intelligence (AI) segment -- dubbed Super Intelligence (SI) -- was particularly impressive. SpaceX's total revenue grew 161% year over year to $14.6 billion, while SI revenue soared 830% year over year to $7.6 billion.

During the third quarter, SpaceX's capex in its SI business was $16.4 billion, up 245.5% year over year. At least some of that money is likely landing right in Nvidia's pockets, as SpaceX continues to expand its capacity to meet the high demand for AI compute. This isn't just speculation either.

SpaceX's management pointed out, among other things, that even older Nvidia systems, like the H100 GPU ( graphics processing unit ), are renting out at a premium compared to when they were new -- the H100 launched in 2022.

That says a lot about Nvidia, and it strongly suggests that newer systems, like the company's Vera Rubin architecture, are experiencing even higher demand. Further, SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk , predicted a shortage of superintelligence compute that would last for some time.

If true, this would certainly benefit Nvidia, potentially granting the company even more pricing power. The bottom line is that while some people still expect the AI bubble to burst and take Nvidia down with it, there is significant evidence that AI infrastructure spending could continue to grow unabated for the foreseeable future. SpaceX gave us more data confirming that.

Meanwhile, Nvidia remains the undisputed leader in GPUs and has significantly expanded its portfolio. The company is well-positioned to tap into the massive demand for AI compute in the medium term and could deliver outstanding returns. In short, it's still not too late to invest in Nvidia, even after its amazing performance over the past five years.

CoreWeave also rents out AI compute capacity through a network of data centers. Some investors are skeptical of the company's prospects right now, but it isn't because sales growth hasn't been impressive. In the second quarter, CoreWeave's revenue increased by 112.5% year over year to $2.6 billion.

CoreWeave ended the period with a revenue backlog of $104 billion, up 245.5% year over year. And that didn't include the more than $25 billion in revenue backlog it recorded in the first few weeks of the third quarter.
However, CoreWeave is incurring significant debt to fund its AI ambitions, which is a meaningful risk investors will need to keep in mind, in addition to the company's customer concentration.

With that said, SpaceX's recent results and management commentary suggest that the kinds of services CoreWeave offers will remain in high demand for a while, which makes its debt-related problems much less concerning.

Consider, for instance, that Musk said that SpaceX could rent out AI compute capacity several times over if the company accepted every request. In other words, current demand significantly exceeds capacity. Also, SpaceX's CFO, Bret Johnsen, noted that "At current pricing, new compute deployments are generating a payback of less than a year."

These are incredibly bullish signs for CoreWeave. And they arguably justify the company spending fortunes to increase its compute capacity. The stock is a bit riskier due to the issues mentioned above. However, it could deliver outstanding returns over the next five years.

Next, it would have to close above the $83,556 level from October's open, then break through $84,856 while oil prices drop back below $100.
On the downside, if Bitcoin closes below the 30-day low of $79,676—only 1.1% lower—while outflows continue, a return to $85,000 may slip into December or later.
It is possible, but it may only be short-lived.
We believe Bitcoin could reach above $85,000—a 5.6% rise—at some point in November since it has already reached $87,249 in the past 30 days.
However, the likelihood of it holding this level through the November 30 close seems low unless ETF inflows start trending positively.
Historically, November has seen both upward and downward swings for Bitcoin.
In November 2024, it opened at $70,347 and closed at $96,436, marking a 37.1% increase.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) approached $85,000, falling about $150 short during the week, before sellers pushed the price down.
Throughout the week, it has fluctuated between a high of $84,856 and a low of $80,401.
Since then, Bitcoin has slipped below that range.
On October 19 and October 21, they saw net inflows of $526.6 million and $528.4 million, respectively, according to SoSoValue.
As of October 22, cumulative net inflows totaled $57.3 billion.
A few days of strong inflows could signal that buyers are ready to propel Bitcoin past $85,000.
A moving average represents the average closing price over a specific period, and when Bitcoin closes above these averages, it often suggests buyers are gaining control.

If the results align closely with these percentages, market uncertainty may ease.
However, unexpected results could increase market volatility.

Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) approached $85,000, falling about $150 short during the week, before sellers pushed the price down . As of the morning of October 24, the Bitcoin price stands at $80,530, reflecting a 3.5% decrease in October. Throughout the week, it has fluctuated between a high of $84,856 and a low of $80,401.

The market continues to test the $85,000 mark, with Bitcoin hitting a 30-day peak of $87,249. On the October 17 episode of The Pomp Podcast , host Anthony Pompliano noted that Bitcoin had been fluctuating between $82,000 and $85,000 while stock prices fell. Since then, Bitcoin has slipped below that range.
The question now is whether Bitcoin can reclaim the $85,000 level in November, and what conditions would need to change for that to happen.

Bitcoin is trading below its 50-day average of $81,776 and its 20-day average of $82,826. A moving average represents the average closing price over a specific period, and when Bitcoin closes above these averages, it often suggests buyers are gaining control.

Next, Bitcoin needs to overcome the October open of $83,556, which is 3.8% above its current price, to erase October’s losses. It must also push past the week’s high of $84,856, a price level where sellers have previously stepped in.

A single strong trading day could help Bitcoin break through all these levels. However, buyers who bought near these levels may sell as soon as they break even. An analyst known as Financelot mentioned on X on October 23 that Bitcoin may have bottomed out earlier than expected and is struggling to overcome its 60-week average.

Historically, November has seen both upward and downward swings for Bitcoin. In November 2024, it opened at $70,347 and closed at $96,436, marking a 37.1% increase. Conversely, in November 2025, it opened at $109,556, dipped to $80,525, and closed at $90,370, a 17.5% loss.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs , which hold Bitcoin and trade like stocks, experienced significant net outflows of $635.6 million on October 22, indicating that investors withdrew more money than they invested. The iShares Bitcoin Trust ( NASDAQ:IBIT ) recorded another $110.3 million in net outflows on October 23.

However, these funds can shift quickly . On October 19 and October 21, they saw net inflows of $526.6 million and $528.4 million, respectively, according to SoSoValue. As of October 22, cumulative net inflows totaled $57.3 billion. A few days of strong inflows could signal that buyers are ready to propel Bitcoin past $85,000.

High oil prices and weak tech stock performance are weighing on Bitcoin. On October 20, WTI crude oil, the U.S. benchmark, traded at $108 a barrel, up 13.1% in a week after peaking at $110 on October 19. About a month earlier, oil prices were at $85. High oil prices contribute to inflation, which often puts downward pressure on speculative assets like Bitcoin.

This pressure remains present, as oil prices rose again on October 23 amid concerns about a wider conflict in the Middle East, and the Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) dropped 5% over the month leading up to October 23. Bitcoin tends to mirror tech stocks, particularly during periods of market uncertainty.

One positive factor has emerged. The 10-year Treasury yield , the government’s long-term borrowing rate, fell to 4.96% on October 22 from 5.31% on October 5. Lower yields typically make riskier investments like Bitcoin more appealing.

Elections are scheduled for November 3, with Polymarket showing the Democratic Party at 91.5% to win the House and 67.5% to win the Senate as of today. If the results align closely with these percentages, market uncertainty may ease. However, unexpected results could increase market volatility.
The VIX, a measure of market volatility, rose to 19 on October 22, up 15.6% in a week. This metric is slightly below the 20-point level, where markets typically become anxious .

It is possible, but it may only be short-lived. We believe Bitcoin could reach above $85,000—a 5.6% rise—at some point in November since it has already reached $87,249 in the past 30 days. However, the likelihood of it holding this level through the November 30 close seems low unless ETF inflows start trending positively.

Bitcoin first needs to surpass both moving averages, then post a series of positive ETF inflow days after the November 3 vote. Next, it would have to close above the $83,556 level from October’s open, then break through $84,856 while oil prices drop back below $100. On the downside, if Bitcoin closes below the 30-day low of $79,676—only 1.1% lower—while outflows continue, a return to $85,000 may slip into December or later.

So, over the next few quarters, watch whether producer prices keep climbing if the Fed starts cutting rates, as that mix of conditions will be a test for Bitcoin's inflation-hedge thesis.

Consumer prices rose by 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and Bitcoin fell about $1,000 on the hotter-than-expected Oct.
14 report, as hot inflation raises the odds of interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Bitcoin.
Still, there's an argument for why more inflation could be bullish for Bitcoin, so let's think about it a bit more.
So, over the next few quarters, watch whether producer prices keep climbing if the Fed starts cutting rates, as that mix of conditions will be a test for Bitcoin's inflation-hedge thesis.
If the coin gains in value, it's likely to protect against inflation at least somewhat.
Morgan Asset Management's 2027 outlook portrays Bitcoin as a bet that governments will continue to create more money, diluting the value of the existing money in circulation.
Its report says that the coin typically behaves as a risky asset that tracks the global money supply.
For now, the Fed is moving in the opposite direction, with markets expecting it to raise rates again before the end of the year.
Bitcoin is not necessarily well suited for benefiting from any of these types of inflation.
Nonetheless, Bitcoin could still benefit from inflation stemming from a different source.
If people's wallets are squeezed, the odds are that many of them will invest less, especially in riskier assets like Bitcoin.

Still, there's an argument for why more inflation could be bullish for Bitcoin, so let's think about it a bit more. The Producer Price Index (PPI) is a measure of inflation that captures the prices companies receive for the goods and services they sell, before those products reach consumers; eventually, those higher costs are usually passed on to consumers in large part. sources.title: Bitcoin Firm Strive Unveils Daily Dividend Payments for SATA Preferred Shares - Yahoo Finance
passages: Strive shares jumped more than 5% to a recent price of $17.60, according to Yahoo Finance , after touching a high of $18.22 earlier Thursday.
Since the company announced its first Bitcoin purchase just over eight months ago, shares have plunged 86% from $130, facing volatility as the digital asset has fallen about 35% from all-time highs.
Strive's preferred stock will soon become the first U.S.-listed security to provide investors with daily cash dividends, the Bitcoin-buying firm declared on Thursday.
SATA, which debuted on the Nasdaq in November, currently carries a stated annual dividend rate of 13%.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Although Strive had issued long-term notes to purchase more Bitcoin than it could otherwise, the firm said on Thursday that it had repurchased them, eliminating outstanding debt.
In the presentation, Strive said SATA had become its only form of Bitcoin-backed "amplification."
The transition underscores continued experimentation among Bitcoin-buying firms that have embraced dividend-paying products as a way to grow their stockpiles.
Strive modeled SATA on Strategy's STRC, which debuted in July and currently pays out 11.5% monthly.
Strive telegraphed SATA's shift alongside first-quarter earnings.
Holding 15,009 Bitcoin on its balance sheet, Strive is the ninth-largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, according to Bitcoin Treasuries.
Strive unveiled its first acquisition in September.
In a statement, CEO Matt Cole described the shift as a "zero-to-one innovation," affecting the company's Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Preferred Stock (SATA) starting June 16.
Last month, Strategy announced a proposed shareholder vote to double the dividend payment frequency on STRC to a semi-monthly schedule, a move aimed at reducing its volatility.
So far this year, Strategy has raised billions of dollars via the dividend-paying product.
Strategy Resumes Bitcoin Buys as Saylor Shifts Focus to 'Never Be a Net Seller'

The securities, which sit between debt and common equity in the capital structure with regular payouts and no voting rights, have financed purchases of some 136,000 bitcoin in the 20 months since their introduction, Fidelity research analyst Zack Wainwright wrote in a Tuesday report . That’s more than 0.5% of the cryptocurrency’s maximum supply.

Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, is the dominant company in the market. Its preferred shares — it has five different classes — make it a bellwether for the model’s durability. Its first offering, STRK, debuted in February 2025.
Fidelity puts the bitcoin-focused preferred market at roughly $12 billion. The global fixed-income market is $150 trillion, suggesting there’s room for growth.
By selling preferred shares that offer dividends without a fixed maturity, the companies reduce refinancing pressure while attracting investors reluctant to own bitcoin directly.
“Perpetual preferreds have brought bitcoin to income investors, a group that ETFs never reached,” said Mark Palmer, a senior equity research analyst at StoneX.

Ryan Rasmussen, the head of research at Bitwise, also sees the products attracting buyers who might avoid bitcoin exchange-traded funds, though he expects the ETFs to remain the bigger demand channel.

“Over the long run, I expect ETFs to be a larger source of demand for bitcoin, with perpetual preferred offerings acting as a second tailwind addressing a different type of investor (yield investors),” Rasmussen said.

James Butterfill, CoinShares’ head of research, said STRC alone, which pays a variable dividend currently around 12% , raised $7.5 billion during 2026 through late July. That funding carries a recurring dividend cost.

Alex Blume, the founder and CEO of institutional bitcoin asset manager Two Prime, pointed out that products such as STRC and Strive’s SATA don’t offer just exposure to bitcoin prices. Their price also reacts to management competence, issuers’ obligations and capital-market conditions.

He cited STRC briefly falling into the $70 range in late June as evidence of potential volatility. Growing issuance creates a tension between increasing bitcoin per common share, meeting dollar-denominated dividend-payout commitments and avoiding bitcoin sales, he said. The Strategy preferred stock currently trades around $99.40.

“The catch is that the demand for perpetual preferreds is reflexive,” Palmer said. Continued preferred-funded buying depends on the securities trading at or near par, he added. Below par, fresh issuance becomes less attractive, and companies may favor repurchases, Butterfill said.

Strategy’s latest weekly update reported $193 million spent repurchasing STRC alongside purchases of just 267 bitcoin, according to Butterfill. The firm also increased its preferred-stock repurchase authorization to $3 billion, he said.
“Buybacks can reduce future dividend costs, but they compete with bitcoin purchases for capital today,” Butterfill said.
Cash reserves provide a buffer, although Strategy has already sold some bitcoin to fund preferred dividends, he added.
U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have attracted approximately $57 billion in cumulative net inflows and hold around $106 billion in assets, Butterfill said.

Net ETF creations increase funds’ bitcoin holdings, while issuance of preferred stock gives management discretion over spending. Redemptions can reverse ETF demand but leave no continuing dividend commitment, he said.
Butterfill sees preferreds amplifying the cycle: supporting purchases when financing conditions are favorable, with that support weakening as sentiment deteriorates.

coreStoryFacts.text: Strive shares jumped more than 5% to a recent price of $17.60, according to Yahoo Finance , after touching a high of $18.22 earlier Thursday.
Since the company announced its first Bitcoin purchase just over eight months ago, shares have plunged 86% from $130, facing volatility as the digital asset has fallen about 35% from all-time highs.
Strive's preferred stock will soon become the first U.S.-listed security to provide investors with daily cash dividends, the Bitcoin-buying firm declared on Thursday.
SATA, which debuted on the Nasdaq in November, currently carries a stated annual dividend rate of 13%.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Although Strive had issued long-term notes to purchase more Bitcoin than it could otherwise, the firm said on Thursday that it had repurchased them, eliminating outstanding debt.
In the presentation, Strive said SATA had become its only form of Bitcoin-backed "amplification."
The transition underscores continued experimentation among Bitcoin-buying firms that have embraced dividend-paying products as a way to grow their stockpiles.
Strive modeled SATA on Strategy's STRC, which debuted in July and currently pays out 11.5% monthly.
Strive telegraphed SATA's shift alongside first-quarter earnings.
Holding 15,009 Bitcoin on its balance sheet, Strive is the ninth-largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, according to Bitcoin Treasuries.
Strive unveiled its first acquisition in September.
In a statement, CEO Matt Cole described the shift as a "zero-to-one innovation," affecting the company's Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Preferred Stock (SATA) starting June 16.
Last month, Strategy announced a proposed shareholder vote to double the dividend payment frequency on STRC to a semi-monthly schedule, a move aimed at reducing its volatility.
So far this year, Strategy has raised billions of dollars via the dividend-paying product.

extraction.body: Bitcoin BTC $84,459.46 treasury companies like Strategy (MSTR) and Strive (ASST), whose purchases help maintain demand for the largest cryptocurrency, have a tough balancing act, according to Fidelity Digital Assets and analysts who spoke to CoinDesk. On the one hand, they need cash to fund their purchases. On the other, they need to maintain investor appetite for new sales of the perpetual preferred stock that is their favored fundraising vehicle. As the number of shares in circulation grows, so do the dividend payments. The securities, which sit between debt and common equity in the capital structure with regular payouts and no voting rights, have financed purchases of some 136,000 bitcoin in the 20 months since their introduction, Fidelity research analyst Zack Wainwright wrote in a Tuesday report . That’s more than 0.5% of the cryptocurrency’s maximum supply. Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, is the dominant company in the market. Its preferred shares — it has five different classes — make it a bellwether for the model’s durability. Its first offering, STRK, debuted in February 2025. Fidelity puts the bitcoin-focused preferred market at roughly $12 billion. The global fixed-income market is $150 trillion, suggesting there’s room for growth. By selling preferred shares that offer dividends without a fixed maturity, the companies reduce refinancing pressure while attracting investors reluctant to own bitcoin directly. “Perpetual preferreds have brought bitcoin to income investors, a group that ETFs never reached,” said Mark Palmer, a senior equity research analyst at StoneX. Ryan Rasmussen, the head of research at Bitwise, also sees the products attracting buyers who might avoid bitcoin exchange-traded funds, though he expects the ETFs to remain the bigger demand channel. “Over the long run, I expect ETFs to be a larger source of demand for bitcoin, with perpetual preferred offerings acting as a second tailwind addressing a different type of investor (yield investors),” Rasmussen said. James Butterfill, CoinShares’ head of research, said STRC alone, which pays a variable dividend currently around 12% , raised $7.5 billion during 2026 through late July. That funding carries a recurring dividend cost. Alex Blume, the founder and CEO of institutional bitcoin asset manager Two Prime, pointed out that products such as STRC and Strive’s SATA don’t offer just exposure to bitcoin prices. Their price also reacts to management competence, issuers’ obligations and capital-market conditions. He cited STRC briefly falling into the $70 range in late June as evidence of potential volatility. Growing issuance creates a tension between increasing bitcoin per common share, meeting dollar-denominated dividend-payout commitments and avoiding bitcoin sales, he said. The Strategy preferred stock currently trades around $99.40. “The catch is that the demand for perpetual preferreds is reflexive,” Palmer said. Continued preferred-funded buying depends on the securities trading at or near par, he added. Below par, fresh issuance becomes less attractive, and companies may favor repurchases, Butterfill said. Strategy’s latest weekly update reported $193 million spent repurchasing STRC alongside purchases of just 267 bitcoin, according to Butterfill. The firm also increased its preferred-stock repurchase authorization to $3 billion, he said. “Buybacks can reduce future dividend costs, but they compete with bitcoin purchases for capital today,” Butterfill said. Cash reserves provide a buffer, although Strategy has already sold some bitcoin to fund preferred dividends, he added. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs have attracted approximately $57 billion in cumulative net inflows and hold around $106 billion in assets, Butterfill said. Net ETF creations increase funds’ bitcoin holdings, while issuance of preferred stock gives management discretion over spending. Redemptions can reverse ETF demand but leave no continuing dividend commitment, he said. Butterfill sees preferreds amplifying the cycle: supporting purchases when financing conditions are favorable, with that support weakening as sentiment deteriorates. extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls .
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.
It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text.
Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard.
Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages.
Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.
There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.
Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.
According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.
The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.
In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

candidate.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.

sources.title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
passages: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will.

A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%.
Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.
Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races.
The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI.
President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions.

The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.
The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]?

Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.
The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh.
GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.
ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely.
Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.
Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.
Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart.
Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans.
There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides.
Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.
The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.

Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots. There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them. “ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.” Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions. “It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics. “If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said. Previous research has raised similar concerns. The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing. The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt. Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%. GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.) The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy. ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans. The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote. Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72. “If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said. One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights. Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat. When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.” The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine. Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections. In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. extraction.body: It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone. For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable , or a new notch on the screen , but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was. The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad. But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO. The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. passages: It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone.

For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable , or a new notch on the screen , but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was.
The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting.

It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.

Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad.
But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO.

The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves.
Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple.

The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think.

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player.
The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.

I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH

Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.
The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show.

Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee.
