As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad. But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO. The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player. This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls. Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it. MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1 Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends. Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken. Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience. I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid. We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead. extraction.body: I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable. Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset. Battlefleet Duo Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip. As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment. RectoVerso: Flashcards Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.” PianoFold Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. Toastie When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

extraction.body: I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable. Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset. Battlefleet Duo Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip. As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment. RectoVerso: Flashcards Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.” PianoFold Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. Toastie When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

extraction.body: Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down . Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December. extraction.body: Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. passages: Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles.
It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened.
Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple.
Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5.
The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023.
Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now.

extraction.body: It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro. There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August. A touchscreen MacBook Pro A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line. This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year. M6 MacBook Pro That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model. OLED iPad Mini Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

extraction.body: It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro. There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August. A touchscreen MacBook Pro A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line. This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year. M6 MacBook Pro That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model. OLED iPad Mini Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

sources.title: I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
passages: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook.
After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh.

I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support.
My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive.
And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor.
Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.

extraction.body: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook. Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs. The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse. [Image: 2-in-1s can be seen as a weird compromise between laptops and tablets. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky. My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

sources.title: These clever apps show off the iPhone Duo’s potential
passages: I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo.
Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.
Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen.
I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential.
Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered?
Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).
The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP.
The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why.
This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure.

Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others.
But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV.

On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display.
The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.
The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band.
When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman.
The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.
If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display.
You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.
Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone.
Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.
I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself.
The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH
Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.
Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.
Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that.
Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.

extraction.body: The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman. The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives. Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun. Duo-Man is now Deck-Man! Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that. See you October 23 on the App Store! pic.twitter.com/kCdjcmbeGG The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed. Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut. You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.) If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player. This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls. Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it. MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1 Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.

extraction.body: The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. extraction.body: U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday. A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu. Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report. The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month. Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026 , allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield. According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement: “Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.” A Google spokesperson tells Ars that its privacy clarification does not indicate a change in how it handles your data with respect to its advertising partners. It’s not scanning your entire inbox to enhance your advertising profile, and it’s not giving any of this data to third parties. But if you pipe personal data into an AI search tool, the ads it shows you could be based on that information. The core of the problem is that Google wants its products and services to talk to each other. Google sees that wealth of data as a key strength of its AI efforts. Some apps like Gmail are still given protected status in Google’s data handling, but there are now more avenues for that data to get out. The more data you share across Google’s ecosystem, the greater the risk to your privacy. We’ve seen a similar exception in the way Google uses your AI interactions for model training . While Google says it doesn’t use personal data for AI training, it does use your inputs and the model outputs for that purpose. With Gemini integrated with so many services and connected to them via Personal Intelligence, those outputs may very well contain elements of your personal information. sources.title: NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France game - The Guardian
passages: Security concerns have overshadowed the NFL’s debut in Paris.
The New Orleans Saints will play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in the league’s first regular-season game in France.
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said this week that preparations had been made in consultation with US and French authorities.
Street protests, he said, “are not unusual in France”.
“It doesn’t feel calm and good to be a tourist in Paris,” he said.
“My cousin is Hungarian, so he knows that the protests happen regularly in Paris.”
Paris braces for protests amid heavy police presence
Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday that he was confident the game would go ahead as planned.
“I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” the four-time MVP said.
If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.”
Live: Thousands march in Paris and other French cities

The league announced the closure to fans on Saturday morning through its “OnePass” app, a day after saying its pop-up NFL shop would also be shut on Saturday – in both cases citing “potential accessibility issues”.

Security concerns have overshadowed the NFL’s debut in Paris. The New Orleans Saints will play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in the league’s first regular-season game in France. Also on Saturday, the Saints announced that “Saints House has been postponed until Sunday.” Events planned for Saturday at NFL House included “French Athletes in Football” and “From the Field to the Community”. “I was looking forward to just checking out some of the installations they had – they were going to have the Lombardi Trophy,” fan Nick Paiva said. Major museums, including the Louvre and the Musée d’Orsay, were closed on Saturday, though tourists lined up to enter Notre Dame Cathedral. French authorities were intent on preventing a repeat of recent violent unrest. The disorder has also disrupted French football, with Sunday’s Ligue 1 match between Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon postponed until Monday at the request of local police, who cited security concerns and the strain on resources. The US state department issued a security alert this week cautioning “Americans in Paris for the NFL game” to “exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings” because of protests. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell said this week that preparations had been made in consultation with US and French authorities. Street protests, he said, “are not unusual in France”. Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said on Friday that he was confident the game would go ahead as planned. “I definitely think that the NFL is alert to what’s going on,” the four-time MVP said. “This game means a lot to the NFL. If it was unsafe, then I’m sure we wouldn’t be here.” On Friday, French president Emmanuel Macron met Goodell, Saints owner Gayle Benson and Steelers owner Art Rooney II at the Élysée Palace to “discuss Sunday’s game and the long-term future of the NFL in Paris”. The NFL said on Friday that its pop-up shop in the city center would be closed on Saturday but that fans could use an alternative shop at Stade de France , north of the city in Saint-Denis. A weekend event for Steelers fans was canceled on Thursday because of security concerns. He had also expected to participate in the league’s “Hail Mary over the Seine” activation, in which fans try to throw a football across the famed waterway near Notre Dame. Despite having registered, Paiva was told at the site that he also needed to have reserved a time slot. “That was not communicated very well,” he said after being turned away. “C’est comme ça – it’s the way it is.” French teenager Oskar Le Gall, wearing a Bryce Young jersey, was able to give it a shot. His throw came up a little short. A worker on the other side stayed busy scooping balls out of the river with a long pole fitted with a net. Le Gall, who is from Brittany, said “the atmosphere of the NFL in Paris is amazing”, noting that French sports leagues and teams typically do not promote themselves as extensively. Le Gall and his brother were keeping an eye on the planned route of Saturday’s protests. “It doesn’t feel calm and good to be a tourist in Paris,” he said. “It’s not good for the NFL.” At one point during the Hail Mary event, 11 national police vans with their emergency lights flashing drove past on the street above as a fan prepared to throw a ball. Steelers fan Monika Allen was able to avoid any protests thanks to advice posted in fan-led Facebook groups. “The fans are doing a good job keeping each other informed of where to be and where not to be,” Allen said near the Hail Mary event. Her cousin, Viktor Toth, was wearing her black Terry Bradshaw Steelers jersey. “We’re not worried,” she said. “My cousin is Hungarian, so he knows that the protests happen regularly in Paris.”

extraction.body: It’s not for the goodness of politicians' hearts that university fees in France are still $200 for a bachelor's degree but thanks to a population that refuses to back down when their rights are being threatened. I have seen many large-scale gatherings during my years in France, but nothing like what’s unfolding right now. Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous France protests, whether it’s the country winning a football match or students fighting for their rights. If you're visiting Paris soon or planning an upcoming trip, here's what to know. With further demonstrations planned for Saturday October 24, the government is preparing a substantial security operation in central Paris that will deploy armored vehicles, specialist police and gendarmerie units, and military personnel from Operation Sentinelle. Closures and curfews On Thursday October 22, the Préfecture de Police banned unauthorized demonstrations and gatherings between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. in several parts of central Paris, including areas around the Louvre, Champs-Élysées, Élysée Palace, Bastille, République, and major railway stations. These closures follow restrictions earlier in the week at major transport interchanges, including République and Châtelet-Les Halles, where trains were unable to stop. Beyond Paris, localized curfews have been introduced in several other French cities, including Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, and Nice. Are protests spreading to other parts of France? Paris is far from the only French city to have been affected by the recent unrest. On Saturday October 17, demonstrations took place across the country, with an estimated 550,000 people taking to the streets according to the French authorities, although organizers put the figure at 800,000. One such incident took place at Place Bellecour, where a branch of the city's tourist office was vandalized and set on fire after a group entered without authorization. Dozens of shops across the Presqu'île, Lyon's central peninsula, were also damaged and looted, while in Limoges, the historic Hôtel de Ville was devastated by a fire during the unrest. Elsewhere, protesters made their way into Marseille's town hall, damaging the interior, while similar incidents were reported at municipal buildings in Lille and Angers. This violence has raised concerns within France's tourism industry, particularly as the country enters the Toussaint school holidays. According to Le Monde, some hotels have already reported cancellations and early departures, although the overall impact on bookings remains limited for now. Does this mean Paris—and France as a whole—is a no-go zone? Certain streets and neighborhoods may be affected by demonstrations, police operations, or temporary closures, but the disruption is not necessarily city-wide. You can still come to Paris during this time and enjoy yourself, provided you keep informed and keep your wits about you when navigating the city. You might have to change some of your plans, but the good thing about Paris is that you can be here for decades, like me, and still discover new beautiful corners. Choose your neighborhood wisely When visiting a city, we all tend to want to stay as central as possible, but this is not always a good idea when protests are happening. Avoid booking a hotel close to main squares or places of particular significance such as République, Bastille, Nation, and Place de Clichy. Paris is not big and quite easy to navigate from wherever you are—at this time, choose to stay in quieter, residential areas. If a primary transportation route becomes inaccessible, do they know how to reach their accommodations or contact someone for assistance?” says John Gobbels, CEO of air medical transport and security response membership program Medjet. “Maintaining situational awareness and having a contingency plan can make a meaningful difference when circumstances change unexpectedly.” Stay informed Although authorized peaceful demonstrations are planned in advance, looters do not give a heads up before they take to the streets, so make sure you keep an eye on French news. “Once in the country, travelers should check local news, government travel advisories, and transport updates before heading out, particularly when demonstrations are expected near major attractions or transport hubs," suggests Gobbels. ”Keep your phone charged, save emergency contacts offline, and be prepared to adjust your itinerary as conditions warrant. If you encounter a demonstration, avoid the crowd, move away calmly, and follow local authorities’ instruction.” For metro closures and issues with public transport, check the Bonjour RATP website, while the Préfecture de Police also publishes information about demonstrations, traffic restrictions, and security measures—it’s worth following on social media platforms for immediate information. Keep your itinerary flexible I know it’s sad not to be able to stick to your plans, but for your safety, it is better to avoid certain areas and attractions while the France protests are unfolding. Big institutions like the Louvre—which was blocked by students on Monday October 19—and the Élysée Palace are better avoided; instead, visit some of the city's niche sights and smaller museums. You could visit the beautiful Musée Gustave Moreau in the 9th or the Musée Zadkine in the 6th, depending on where you are staying. Big touristy spots such as the Eiffel Tower are open and busy—if you don’t feel comfortable but still want a picture with the monument in the background, head to Île aux Cygnes to see the tiny Statue of Liberty and the Tower in all her glory, from a safe distance. A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

sources.title: Is it Safe to Travel to Paris Right Now Amidst the France Protests?
passages: Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous France protests, whether it’s the country winning a football match or students fighting for their rights.
I have seen many large-scale gatherings during my years in France, but nothing like what’s unfolding right now.
Are protests spreading to other parts of France?
Does this mean Paris—and France as a whole—is a no-go zone?
sources.body: Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous France protests, whether it’s the country winning a football match or students fighting for their rights. Does this mean Paris—and France as a whole—is a no-go zone?

extraction.body: It’s not for the goodness of politicians' hearts that university fees in France are still $200 for a bachelor's degree but thanks to a population that refuses to back down when their rights are being threatened. I have seen many large-scale gatherings during my years in France, but nothing like what’s unfolding right now. Although not always of this magnitude, violence and looting have also marred some previous France protests, whether it’s the country winning a football match or students fighting for their rights. If you're visiting Paris soon or planning an upcoming trip, here's what to know. With further demonstrations planned for Saturday October 24, the government is preparing a substantial security operation in central Paris that will deploy armored vehicles, specialist police and gendarmerie units, and military personnel from Operation Sentinelle. Closures and curfews On Thursday October 22, the Préfecture de Police banned unauthorized demonstrations and gatherings between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. in several parts of central Paris, including areas around the Louvre, Champs-Élysées, Élysée Palace, Bastille, République, and major railway stations. These closures follow restrictions earlier in the week at major transport interchanges, including République and Châtelet-Les Halles, where trains were unable to stop. Beyond Paris, localized curfews have been introduced in several other French cities, including Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, and Nice. Are protests spreading to other parts of France? Paris is far from the only French city to have been affected by the recent unrest. On Saturday October 17, demonstrations took place across the country, with an estimated 550,000 people taking to the streets according to the French authorities, although organizers put the figure at 800,000. One such incident took place at Place Bellecour, where a branch of the city's tourist office was vandalized and set on fire after a group entered without authorization. Dozens of shops across the Presqu'île, Lyon's central peninsula, were also damaged and looted, while in Limoges, the historic Hôtel de Ville was devastated by a fire during the unrest. Elsewhere, protesters made their way into Marseille's town hall, damaging the interior, while similar incidents were reported at municipal buildings in Lille and Angers. This violence has raised concerns within France's tourism industry, particularly as the country enters the Toussaint school holidays. According to Le Monde, some hotels have already reported cancellations and early departures, although the overall impact on bookings remains limited for now. Does this mean Paris—and France as a whole—is a no-go zone? Certain streets and neighborhoods may be affected by demonstrations, police operations, or temporary closures, but the disruption is not necessarily city-wide. You can still come to Paris during this time and enjoy yourself, provided you keep informed and keep your wits about you when navigating the city. You might have to change some of your plans, but the good thing about Paris is that you can be here for decades, like me, and still discover new beautiful corners. Choose your neighborhood wisely When visiting a city, we all tend to want to stay as central as possible, but this is not always a good idea when protests are happening. Avoid booking a hotel close to main squares or places of particular significance such as République, Bastille, Nation, and Place de Clichy. Paris is not big and quite easy to navigate from wherever you are—at this time, choose to stay in quieter, residential areas. If a primary transportation route becomes inaccessible, do they know how to reach their accommodations or contact someone for assistance?” says John Gobbels, CEO of air medical transport and security response membership program Medjet. “Maintaining situational awareness and having a contingency plan can make a meaningful difference when circumstances change unexpectedly.” Stay informed Although authorized peaceful demonstrations are planned in advance, looters do not give a heads up before they take to the streets, so make sure you keep an eye on French news. “Once in the country, travelers should check local news, government travel advisories, and transport updates before heading out, particularly when demonstrations are expected near major attractions or transport hubs," suggests Gobbels. ”Keep your phone charged, save emergency contacts offline, and be prepared to adjust your itinerary as conditions warrant. If you encounter a demonstration, avoid the crowd, move away calmly, and follow local authorities’ instruction.” For metro closures and issues with public transport, check the Bonjour RATP website, while the Préfecture de Police also publishes information about demonstrations, traffic restrictions, and security measures—it’s worth following on social media platforms for immediate information. Keep your itinerary flexible I know it’s sad not to be able to stick to your plans, but for your safety, it is better to avoid certain areas and attractions while the France protests are unfolding. Big institutions like the Louvre—which was blocked by students on Monday October 19—and the Élysée Palace are better avoided; instead, visit some of the city's niche sights and smaller museums. You could visit the beautiful Musée Gustave Moreau in the 9th or the Musée Zadkine in the 6th, depending on where you are staying. Big touristy spots such as the Eiffel Tower are open and busy—if you don’t feel comfortable but still want a picture with the monument in the background, head to Île aux Cygnes to see the tiny Statue of Liberty and the Tower in all her glory, from a safe distance. A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

sources.title: After another day of Paris protests, NFL is on track to stage Steelers-Saints at Stade de France - NBC Sports
passages: With kickoff to Sunday’s game between the Steelers and Saints in Paris less than 13 hours away, as of this posting, the plan continues to be full speed ahead for Steelers-Saints at Stade de France.
Even if the league is potentially going to be stepping into a steaming pile of merde .
ET kickoff after another day of local protests in Paris.
The question remains whether protestors will target the NFL game, in an effort to send a clear international message.
No matter how secure the stadium may be, the path to the venue’s security perimeter may not be.
For the NFL, the necessity to play flows from the ongoing obsession to export the game to other countries.

extraction.body: With kickoff to Sunday’s game between the Steelers and Saints in Paris less than 13 hours away, as of this posting, the plan continues to be full speed ahead for Steelers-Saints at Stade de France. Even if the league is potentially going to be stepping into a steaming pile of merde . Via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports , the game remains set for a 9:30 a.m. ET kickoff after another day of local protests in Paris. More than 400,000 participated in the demonstrations, which resulted in more than 1,000 arrests. Per the Associated Press, a march that started peacefully ended with protesters throwing fireworks and other objects at police . They responded with tear gas, sound grenades, and water cannons. The question remains whether protestors will target the NFL game, in an effort to send a clear international message. No matter how secure the stadium may be, the path to the venue’s security perimeter may not be. Hopefully, there will be no incidents. It’s still a calculated risk for the NFL, one that many would regard as unnecessary. For the NFL, the necessity to play flows from the ongoing obsession to export the game to other countries. If something occurs, it will be impossible for the league to shrug and to say, “We didn’t know that could happen.” And it will throw a wrench into the plan to globalize the game. Even without any specific problems on Sunday, the situation underscores the realities of potentially putting teams in other countries, with other governments and other citizenries that could eventually complicate the effort to play all games as scheduled. For now, the league doesn’t care. It only sees one thing — the possibility of transforming a billion-dollar business into a trillion-dollar behemoth if fans in other countries become as passionate about pro football as Americans are.
