sources.title: Gaming Can’t Afford More Games the Size of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
passages: Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.
Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences.
sources.body: Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences.

extraction.body: It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing. The Human Cost of AAA At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is. On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade. Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition). Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online. With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game. Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them. The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis. It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios. Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches. Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation. A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though). It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch. With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback. Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”) Same Old, Same Old Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games. It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns. However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience. Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost. Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine­—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay. The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways. Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer. But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments. Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2? Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it? Less Is More The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller. That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles. The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded. In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either. It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026. While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff. The game was hugely successful for its budget, letting the studio continue without resorting to painful layoffs. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences. The memory crisis is forcibly extending the hardware life cycle, delaying new console generations and blocking supplies of powerful PC graphics cards, leaving many players without the means to reap the benefits of the most demanding games. As Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi—no stranger to hugely ambitious games with incredibly long development cycles—says, “There isn't a single console that you can say, ‘As long as I have this, I'll be able to play everything, to do everything.’ Personally, I think that over the course of the next 10 years, if someone said, ‘Here's the next generation of consoles,’ the market and the audience are not necessarily going to just jump over.” Hamaguchi says the industry will still straddle the lower-spec options, like a Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch 2, providing broader experiences to a wider base. It won't be so much about cutting-edge technology, but how developers can compete in game design. "I think we're going to be entering an age where that's really the focus of competition,” he says.
passages: It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing.
The Human Cost of AAA At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is.
On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade.
Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition).

Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online.
With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game.

Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.
The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis.

It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios.
Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches.

Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation.
A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though).

It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch.
With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback.

Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”) Same Old, Same Old Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games.
It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns.
However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience.
Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost.

Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine­—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay.
The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways.

Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer.
But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments.
Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2?
Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it?
Less Is More The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller.

That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles.
The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded.
In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either.
It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026.
While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff.

passages: Tonight we'll get probably our best look at Grand Theft Auto 6 yet, as Rockstar's 'extended look' trailer airs exclusively on Netflix.
We'll be watching it live and reporting on everything we see, here, in this article.
GTA 6 was originally Project Americas and covered "big swaths" of country's north and south, Rockstar reveals, in interview tackling crunch, delays, and leaks
We've had two official trailers show us montages of action across Leonidas (the game's version of Florida), but we haven't yet seen - officially - what it's like to play the game.
Unofficially, of course, we have: days of GTA 6 gameplay video leaks have given us a pretty broad idea of what to expect.
But this trailer ought to provide a much more authored and considered look.
"That was not received well at Nintendo" - as GTA 6 and Zelda are lampooned by Saturday Night Live, former employees recall Elon Musk Wario skit controversy
But then, Netflix has to be used to big premieres.
I'm sure the Stranger Things finale had a heavy load, so to speak.
But it'd be entertaining to see GTA rise out of the waters and demolish it.
GTA 6: This is what a billion dollars gets you
GTA 6's PC release date is set for "Q1 2027", per a new report
GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek is back with another video and this time, Lucia's naked
Will the gameplay live up to the hype, though?
I guess they had a case of having so much to show and only 25 minutes to show it.
Would a single mission shown in real-time have had the same effect?
Another part of this is Rockstar - I think it just loves an authored video with good music and careful editing.
Rockstar HR manager claims he had "little interest" in staff's union membership status as fired GTA dev union-busting trial heats up
The question is, what do you watch on Netflix while you're waiting?
Netflix is trying to recommend me a Tekken anime.
And the Tomb Raider animated series, which I've watched a bit of, and wasn't a massive dan of.
A voice over is telling us to enjoy it, enjoy life, take our time.
We see boating and Jason and Lucia hanging out with a beer, with a friend.
I love the fact that, in a silly, knockabout satire take on Florida, Rockstar is playing this part of the game straight.
It's the boldest move the team could have made, I think.
It's fascinating to see the series' skill for observation, often used to skewer culture, being used for this: creating connection and a feeling of intimacy.

extraction.body: Rockstar Games has confirmed an unexpected change from Grand Theft Auto V in GTA 6 . Recently, Rockstar confirmed a substantial upgrade in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . This new change isn’t much of an upgrade, as it is a change. Those who prefer realism, and in particular enjoyed the realism of Red Dead Redemption 2 , may see this change as an upgrade, but those who prefer free-flowing gameplay over realism — well, these GTA fans may see this change as a downgrade. Rockstar Games has always been obsessed with realism, and you really started to see this obsession in design come to fruition in Red Dead Redemption 2 , where the technology and resources began to really facilitate this dedication. In GTA 5 you saw this less, and as a result, more emphasis left on the series’ chaotic open-world sandbox. To this end, we have remarked on numerous occasions GTA 6 is more like RDR2 than GTA 5 . Supporting this thesis, in favor of realism, Rockstar Games has purposefully made the roads more narrow in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . And it has coupled this by adding increased traffic density. As a result, driving in GTA 6 is described as being both more immersive and challenging in GTA 6 . This is all according to Jason Schreier , who recently went hands on with the game. This is great news for those who prefer realism over anything else. This could be problematic for the raw fun factor of the game, though. One of the best parts of the Grand Theft Auto series is driving around its vast open-world, often at incredibly high speeds. If there is more traffic and the roads don’t faciliate this as much, well there is simply going to be less of it. At least this will be the case in Vice City itself. The surronding more rural areas will likely widen and obviously have less traffic getting in your way. Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the best games of all time, and it’s obessive with its pursuit of realism. It fits better with the series’ slower pace, though. Grand Theft Auto is fast, over-the-top, and loud by comparison. Realism suits its DNA worse. This doesn’t mean it won’t work, especially because it remains to be seen just how different it will feel in this regard compared to GTA 5 . It should be stated that everything we’ve seen of GTA 6 so far looks like more Grand Theft Auto , but it does sound more grounded in realism in a way GTA 5 never felt, but we have seen from the series with GTA San Andreas , in particular, but also GTA 4 to an extent. In GTA 5 you saw this less, and as a result, more emphasis left on the series’ chaotic open-world sandbox. To this end, we have remarked on numerous occasions GTA 6 is more like RDR2 than GTA 5 . Supporting this thesis, in favor of realism, Rockstar Games has purposefully made the roads more narrow in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . And it has coupled this by adding increased traffic density. As a result, driving in GTA 6 is described as being both more immersive and challenging in GTA 6 . This is all according to Jason Schreier , who recently went hands on with the game.

This is great news for those who prefer realism over anything else. This could be problematic for the raw fun factor of the game, though. One of the best parts of the Grand Theft Auto series is driving around its vast open-world, often at incredibly high speeds. If there is more traffic and the roads don’t faciliate this as much, well there is simply going to be less of it. At least this will be the case in Vice City itself. The surronding more rural areas will likely widen and obviously have less traffic getting in your way.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the best games of all time, and it’s obessive with its pursuit of realism. It fits better with the series’ slower pace, though. Grand Theft Auto is fast, over-the-top, and loud by comparison. Realism suits its DNA worse. This doesn’t mean it won’t work, especially because it remains to be seen just how different it will feel in this regard compared to GTA 5 .

It should be stated that everything we’ve seen of GTA 6 so far looks like more Grand Theft Auto , but it does sound more grounded in realism in a way GTA 5 never felt, but we have seen from the series with GTA San Andreas , in particular, but also GTA 4 to an extent. To this end, Rockstar Games recently confirmed that a feature from GTA 4 is returning in GTA 6 .

extraction.body: It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing. The Human Cost of AAA At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is. On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade. Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition). Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online. With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game. Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them. The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis. It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios. Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches. Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation. A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though). It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch. With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback. Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”) Same Old, Same Old Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games. It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns. However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience. Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost. Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine­—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay. The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways. Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer. But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments. Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2? Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it? Less Is More The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller. That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles. The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded. In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either. It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026. While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff. The game was hugely successful for its budget, letting the studio continue without resorting to painful layoffs. Look at Supergiant Games’ Hades duology, AdHoc Studio’s Dispatch, or Mintrocket’s Dave the Diver for more evidence that studios and labels should focus on smaller but richer gaming experiences. The memory crisis is forcibly extending the hardware life cycle, delaying new console generations and blocking supplies of powerful PC graphics cards, leaving many players without the means to reap the benefits of the most demanding games. As Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi—no stranger to hugely ambitious games with incredibly long development cycles—says, “There isn't a single console that you can say, ‘As long as I have this, I'll be able to play everything, to do everything.’ Personally, I think that over the course of the next 10 years, if someone said, ‘Here's the next generation of consoles,’ the market and the audience are not necessarily going to just jump over.” Hamaguchi says the industry will still straddle the lower-spec options, like a Steam Deck or Nintendo Switch 2, providing broader experiences to a wider base. It won't be so much about cutting-edge technology, but how developers can compete in game design. "I think we're going to be entering an age where that's really the focus of competition,” he says.
passages: It’s shaping up to be a game of unprecedented scale and ambition—and exactly the sort of experience the wider industry can’t afford to keep chasing.
The Human Cost of AAA At launch, it doesn’t matter how good or bad Grand Theft Auto VI actually is.
On sheer hype alone, it’s already guaranteed to be the biggest and most successful entertainment product of the year, maybe the decade.
Some estimates already put revenue between $1 billion and $4 billion on preorders alone, with eager players clearly not put off by its $80 price (or $100 for the Ultimate Edition).

Although Rockstar hasn’t confirmed the development budget, that would be a healthy return even on the wildest (and debunked) guess of $2 billion, before factoring long-tail sales or the revenue drawn by the ongoing Grand Theft Auto Online.
With numbers like those, it’s easy to understand why every publisher and developer wants their own GTA VI–level game.

Yet even if Grand Theft Auto VI is an outlier, the arms race among AAA-tier developers to constantly deliver bigger, more detailed, more ambitious games is a dangerous direction, hurting both game quality and the people who make them.
The games industry is in a paradoxical crisis.

It’s the most successful entertainment medium on Earth—generating $200 billion in revenue in 2025, dwarfing the global film industry’s $32.8 billion and even beating the combined sports sector's $174 billion—but the last few years have seen seemingly endless developer layoffs, many at headline AAA studios.
Worse, many of these redundancies are coming after successful game launches.

Despite being the top-selling game of the year, shifting 7 million copies in three days after a reported development budget of $400 million, publisher EA fired workers across at least four studios involved in the game's creation.
A spokesperson told IGN that the job losses were made to “better align our teams around what matters most to our community” (the CEO got a nice $8 million bonus, though).

It’s far from the only case—Halo: Campaign Evolved developers Halo Studios faced 268 job losses in September 2026, following Xbox announcing 3,200 cuts in July 2026 as part of a wider “reset” across Xbox, while Ubisoft is hitting at least three of its German studios with a round of “voluntary” layoffs, including its Düsseldorf branch that has worked on the likes of Rainbow Six: Siege, which boasts “more than 100 million registered players.” Smaller studios aren't immune—Refactor Games, behind Netflix’s FIFA World Cup game, lost 85 percent of its staff after a “successful” launch.
With developers facing unemployment threats even after delivering a financially successful game, unionization efforts are unsurprising, though that's seeing pushback.

Rockstar is currently embroiled in a UK tribunal hearing over the alleged dismissal of 34 workers in Edinburgh for union activity. (Rockstar says the workers were dismissed for “sharing confidential company information.”) Same Old, Same Old Beyond a fraught job market and an unpredictable environment to create games, the AAA sector’s endless pursuit of digital perfection is now arguably delivering weaker, blander games.
It’s almost understandable from a financial perspective: If you’ve invested millions of dollars, you want the end product to appeal to the largest possible consumer base to maximize your returns.
However, that same impulse can homogenize the gaming experience.
Think of all the big-budget shooters that play identically, or the glossy adventure games that signpost every step with yellow paint so players can’t possibly get lost.

Look at the likes of Insomniac’s recent Marvel’s Wolverine­—rumored to have a development budget in the hundreds of millions—which launched to solid sales (analyst estimates suggest 1.9 million copies sold in its first three days) but tepid reviews and lukewarm player response, with many critiquing its linear progression and repetitive hack-and-slash gameplay.
The bigger games have gotten, the more time they demand from players too, and rarely in meaningful ways.

Open-world games in particular feel increasingly crammed with time-eating diversions—Assassin’s Creed Valhalla notoriously needed 150-plus hours to see everything its accurately crafted bleak medieval English settlements had to offer.
But much of it felt like busywork to showcase Ubisoft’s investment in creating such realistic environments.
Such virtual spaces are often impressive, yes, but will Grand Theft Auto VI be better with a world map reportedly three times larger than the already colossal Red Dead Redemption 2?
Is it worth building something of that size if players don’t have time to experience most of it?
Less Is More The solution to runaway costs, developer security, and the limited time players have to sink into games should be clear: aim smaller.

That’s not to say the entire industry should pivot toward indie-level games (though there are some absolute greats in that area), but rather that publishers should refocus on games that can still showcase their creators’ talents and offer satisfying but digestible experiences to players, without pouring dangerous sums of money into ever bigger, ever riskier titles.
The debut game from French developer Sandfall Interactive appeared practically out of nowhere in April 2025, and exploded.
In technology and production quality terms, it’s no slouch for a “smaller” game, either.
It ultimately swept up over 500 Game of the Year Awards and went on to sell 8 million copies as of April 2026.
While that number pales in comparison to Battlefield 6’s 7 million units in mere days, Clair Obscur did it all on a budget of less than $10 million, and with a tiny development staff.

passages: Tonight we'll get probably our best look at Grand Theft Auto 6 yet, as Rockstar's 'extended look' trailer airs exclusively on Netflix.
We'll be watching it live and reporting on everything we see, here, in this article.
GTA 6 was originally Project Americas and covered "big swaths" of country's north and south, Rockstar reveals, in interview tackling crunch, delays, and leaks
We've had two official trailers show us montages of action across Leonidas (the game's version of Florida), but we haven't yet seen - officially - what it's like to play the game.
Unofficially, of course, we have: days of GTA 6 gameplay video leaks have given us a pretty broad idea of what to expect.
But this trailer ought to provide a much more authored and considered look.
"That was not received well at Nintendo" - as GTA 6 and Zelda are lampooned by Saturday Night Live, former employees recall Elon Musk Wario skit controversy
But then, Netflix has to be used to big premieres.
I'm sure the Stranger Things finale had a heavy load, so to speak.
But it'd be entertaining to see GTA rise out of the waters and demolish it.
GTA 6: This is what a billion dollars gets you
GTA 6's PC release date is set for "Q1 2027", per a new report
GTA 6 leaker CyberLeek is back with another video and this time, Lucia's naked
Will the gameplay live up to the hype, though?
I guess they had a case of having so much to show and only 25 minutes to show it.
Would a single mission shown in real-time have had the same effect?
Another part of this is Rockstar - I think it just loves an authored video with good music and careful editing.
Rockstar HR manager claims he had "little interest" in staff's union membership status as fired GTA dev union-busting trial heats up
The question is, what do you watch on Netflix while you're waiting?
Netflix is trying to recommend me a Tekken anime.
And the Tomb Raider animated series, which I've watched a bit of, and wasn't a massive dan of.
A voice over is telling us to enjoy it, enjoy life, take our time.
We see boating and Jason and Lucia hanging out with a beer, with a friend.
I love the fact that, in a silly, knockabout satire take on Florida, Rockstar is playing this part of the game straight.
It's the boldest move the team could have made, I think.
It's fascinating to see the series' skill for observation, often used to skewer culture, being used for this: creating connection and a feeling of intimacy.

extraction.body: Rockstar Games has confirmed an unexpected change from Grand Theft Auto V in GTA 6 . Recently, Rockstar confirmed a substantial upgrade in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . This new change isn’t much of an upgrade, as it is a change. Those who prefer realism, and in particular enjoyed the realism of Red Dead Redemption 2 , may see this change as an upgrade, but those who prefer free-flowing gameplay over realism — well, these GTA fans may see this change as a downgrade. Rockstar Games has always been obsessed with realism, and you really started to see this obsession in design come to fruition in Red Dead Redemption 2 , where the technology and resources began to really facilitate this dedication. In GTA 5 you saw this less, and as a result, more emphasis left on the series’ chaotic open-world sandbox. To this end, we have remarked on numerous occasions GTA 6 is more like RDR2 than GTA 5 . Supporting this thesis, in favor of realism, Rockstar Games has purposefully made the roads more narrow in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . And it has coupled this by adding increased traffic density. As a result, driving in GTA 6 is described as being both more immersive and challenging in GTA 6 . This is all according to Jason Schreier , who recently went hands on with the game. This is great news for those who prefer realism over anything else. This could be problematic for the raw fun factor of the game, though. One of the best parts of the Grand Theft Auto series is driving around its vast open-world, often at incredibly high speeds. If there is more traffic and the roads don’t faciliate this as much, well there is simply going to be less of it. At least this will be the case in Vice City itself. The surronding more rural areas will likely widen and obviously have less traffic getting in your way. Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the best games of all time, and it’s obessive with its pursuit of realism. It fits better with the series’ slower pace, though. Grand Theft Auto is fast, over-the-top, and loud by comparison. Realism suits its DNA worse. This doesn’t mean it won’t work, especially because it remains to be seen just how different it will feel in this regard compared to GTA 5 . It should be stated that everything we’ve seen of GTA 6 so far looks like more Grand Theft Auto , but it does sound more grounded in realism in a way GTA 5 never felt, but we have seen from the series with GTA San Andreas , in particular, but also GTA 4 to an extent. In GTA 5 you saw this less, and as a result, more emphasis left on the series’ chaotic open-world sandbox. To this end, we have remarked on numerous occasions GTA 6 is more like RDR2 than GTA 5 . Supporting this thesis, in favor of realism, Rockstar Games has purposefully made the roads more narrow in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 . And it has coupled this by adding increased traffic density. As a result, driving in GTA 6 is described as being both more immersive and challenging in GTA 6 . This is all according to Jason Schreier , who recently went hands on with the game.

This is great news for those who prefer realism over anything else. This could be problematic for the raw fun factor of the game, though. One of the best parts of the Grand Theft Auto series is driving around its vast open-world, often at incredibly high speeds. If there is more traffic and the roads don’t faciliate this as much, well there is simply going to be less of it. At least this will be the case in Vice City itself. The surronding more rural areas will likely widen and obviously have less traffic getting in your way.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is one of the best games of all time, and it’s obessive with its pursuit of realism. It fits better with the series’ slower pace, though. Grand Theft Auto is fast, over-the-top, and loud by comparison. Realism suits its DNA worse. This doesn’t mean it won’t work, especially because it remains to be seen just how different it will feel in this regard compared to GTA 5 .

It should be stated that everything we’ve seen of GTA 6 so far looks like more Grand Theft Auto , but it does sound more grounded in realism in a way GTA 5 never felt, but we have seen from the series with GTA San Andreas , in particular, but also GTA 4 to an extent. To this end, Rockstar Games recently confirmed that a feature from GTA 4 is returning in GTA 6 .

Cooling in sea surface temperatures in the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean will impact weather around the world, especially in North America during the winter months. Here's an outlook for the 2024/2025 winter season. There is higher chances of seeing warmer than normal winter for the entire East Coast -- from Florida to Maine. Mmost of the South and the Southwest will have a higher chance of seeing warmer than normal temperatures from Georgia to Texas and west into Southern California . NOAA forecasts colder than normal conditions from the Pacific Northwest, the northern Rockies and the northern Plains. With colder weather, the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies could see more mountain snow this winter. More than average snowfall is possible for the Great Lakes, especially in Wisconsin and Michigan. There is a chance we could see big lake effect snow events in western New York. It could be snowier than a typical winter for Chicago and Detroit. Most of the South and the Southwest will be below normal for precipitation. There is a higher chance of seeing a drier than normal winter from Florida to Arizona. As a result, NOAA forecasters, in collaboration with the National Integrated Drought Information System, or NIDIS, expect drought conditions to persist and worsen across the central and southern Plains of the U.S. "Unfortunately, after a brief period in the spring of 2024 with minimal drought conditions across the country, more than a quarter of the land mass in the continental U.S. is currently in at least a moderate drought," said Brad Pugh, operational drought lead with NOAA's Climate Prediction Center. "The winter precipitation outlook does not bode well for widespread relief." As for the Northeast, and the I-95 corridor, Washington D.C., Philladelphia , New York and Boston, will be near normal snowfall this winter, meaning there is a better shot than last two years of seeing measurable snow.

Cooling in sea surface temperatures in the equatorial eastern Pacific Ocean will impact weather around the world, especially in North America during the winter months. With colder weather, the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies could see more mountain snow this winter. More than average snowfall is possible for the Great Lakes, especially in Wisconsin and Michigan. There is a chance we could see big lake effect snow events in western New York. It could be snowier than a typical winter for Chicago and Detroit. Most of the South and the Southwest will be below normal for precipitation. There is a higher chance of seeing a drier than normal winter from Florida to Arizona. As for the Northeast, and the I-95 corridor, Washington D.C., Philladelphia , New York and Boston, will be near normal snowfall this winter, meaning there is a better shot than last two years of seeing measurable snow.
